title: Chinese Parts Are Fuelling Houthi Bid to Build Missiles That Reach Israel, Saudi Arabia
excerpt: Intercepted shipments of Chinese missile motors, fins and heat-shield material point to a Houthi effort to build a version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan, though how far production has advanced is unclear.
body:
• A Conflict Armament Research report, reported by The Wall Street Journal, says Yemeni authorities intercepted two shipments last year containing Chinese-made components for a missile modelled on Iran's Kheibar Shekan.
  • The Kheibar Shekan has a reported range of about 2,000 km (roughly 1,200 miles), which would place all of Saudi Arabia and Israel within reach of a Houthi-built version.
  • A separate Bloomberg investigation traced four containers seized at Aden containing suspected missile parts, drone components and machine tools shipped from China toward Houthi-controlled Hodeidah.
  • China has said it complies with the UN arms embargo on the Houthis and maintains controls on military and dual-use exports; neither report establishes direct Chinese government involvement.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are seeking to manufacture advanced ballistic missiles using components sourced from China, according to a new report by Conflict Armament Research (CAR) reported by The Wall Street Journal via Newsmax. A separate Bloomberg investigation documented a wider supply network bringing missile parts and drone components into Yemen. Together, the findings suggest the Houthis are trying to build more of their own weapons rather than relying primarily on Iran — though how far that effort has progressed remains uncertain.

What the intercepted shipments contained

CAR, a group that traces weapons supply chains in conflict zones, based its findings on information Yemeni authorities provided in July about two shipments intercepted last year. The cargo included custom-made metal parts for missile motors and airframes, stabilising fins and solid-propellant rocket motor components for a missile modelled on Iran's Kheibar Shekan. Investigators also identified heat-shield material, tools and testing equipment. Some components were specifically designed for missile production; others had potential civilian applications.

https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2110201575050248421

The Kheibar Shekan, first revealed by Iran in 2022, has a reported range of around 2,000 km, potentially placing all of Saudi Arabia and Israel within reach. Its manoeuvrability is intended to make interception by air-defence systems more difficult.

"When you have imports like that, there is a possibility that they are already manufacturing or that they are trying and it doesn't really work out."

— Fabian Hinz, Senior Analyst, Conflict Armament Research

Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at CAR, told the Journal the components suggested the Houthis were either already manufacturing missiles or attempting to do so, but their concealed facilities made it hard to establish how far production had progressed.

A wider supply network through Aden

Bloomberg's September 23 investigation examined four containers seized at Aden, shipped from China and bound for Houthi-controlled Hodeidah. Experts found suspected missile parts, drone components, control systems, launch equipment, machine tools and tunnelling equipment, including rear fins resembling Iranian ballistic missile components and phenolic resin, used in heat-resistant missile shields.

Fawaz Al Bsesi, director general of Aden's Land, Sea and Air Ports Department, told Bloomberg the components appeared to have been distributed across four containers to make them harder to detect. Shipping records showed dozens of containers moving under 41 bills of lading, with the named Yemeni importer changed in transit in 25 cases — changes Aden authorities said were meant to conceal the Houthi-linked companies behind the shipments.

From Iranian imports to domestic production

The Houthis expanded their arsenal over years of conflict with support from Iran and Lebanon's Hezbollah. Between 2015 and 2019 they relied heavily on importing Iranian missiles in disassembled form; from 2020 to 2023 they increasingly imported components to assemble or upgrade weapons.

Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the US-based security advisory firm Basha Report, told the Journal the Houthis had expanded their supply chains, accumulated operational experience and incorporated artificial intelligence into software for their missiles and drones. Henry Thompson, a former expert on the UN panel monitoring sanctions on Yemen, said there was evidence the group had been importing components for solid-fuel ballistic missiles from China for at least two years, and warned such missiles could strike deeper into Saudi Arabia with larger payloads than cruise missiles and drones.

China's position

China has said it complies with the UN arms embargo on the Houthis and maintains controls on military exports and dual-use goods. The CAR findings identify a Chinese precision-metal producer as a source but do not establish that China's government directed the shipments, and no direct Chinese official response to the CAR report itself was carried in the reporting reviewed for this article. The reports instead raise questions about how specialised components reach the group through commercial supply chains, where dual-use goods can move under ordinary trade paperwork.

Why it matters beyond Yemen

A Houthi force able to manufacture medium-range ballistic missiles at home would be harder to constrain through interdiction alone, and would deepen the threat to Saudi Arabia, Israel and Red Sea shipping. For India, with millions of workers in the Gulf and energy imports transiting these waters, that is a direct economic and security concern.
